titel: Lot selection, transfers and tax deferral
kurz: Which shares count as sold in a partial sale and how to choose them, what happens for tax purposes when you move an account, give shares away or leave them to heirs, and what deferring the tax until the sale is worth.

bloecke.md:
Besides its market value, every taxable portfolio contains a figure that appears on no statement: the **latent tax**. Of every dollar of unrealized long-term gain, about 85 cents belong to you economically at a 15% rate, or about 81 cents if the 3.8% NIIT also applies. The rest is owed to the government, but only when you sell.

There is no holding period after which gains become tax-free; after one year, the rate merely falls from ordinary to long-term. A long holding period therefore mainly postpones the tax. Unlike in many other countries, however, the US offers two ways in which a gain can escape income tax for good: the step-up in basis at death and the donation of appreciated shares to charity. The room for tax planning rests on four levers: which shares you sell, how you move them, when you sell and whether you sell at all.

## Which shares count as sold

If you bought the same security several times, each purchase is a separate lot with its own basis and holding period. When you sell only part of the position, the regulations allow you to choose the lots by specific identification (26 CFR § 1.1012-1(c)). If you do not identify any lots, the shares bought first are treated as sold first. This default is called FIFO, short for “first in, first out”. For mutual fund shares and shares in dividend reinvestment plans, you can also elect the average cost method, and many brokers use it as the default for funds.

Specific identification has to be chosen at the latest when the trade settles. Most brokers let you set a standing method such as “highest cost” or “tax-lot optimizer”, or pick the lots in the order screen; the trade confirmation then documents the choice. You cannot change the lots after the fact, for example when you prepare your return.

An index ETF was bought three times, 100 shares each time. The price today is $160, and you are in the 15% range for long-term gains.

- 100 shares at $50 (2014) = $5,000
- 100 shares at $90 (2019) = $9,000
- 100 shares at $130 (2024) = $13,000

You sell 100 shares for $16,000.

Under FIFO, the 2014 lot counts as sold. The gain is $11,000, and the tax is $1,650.

With specific identification of the 2024 lot, which has also been held for more than one year, the gain is $3,000 and the tax $450.

With the same sale proceeds, the difference is $1,200. If you need $16,000 after tax, you have to sell about 111 shares under FIFO but only about 103 shares with the 2024 lot.

bloecke.md:
## Lots across accounts

You do not need separate accounts to control which lots are sold; specific identification does that within one account. Two cases still need attention. First, if you hold the same security at several brokers, each broker only knows its own lots, and the wash sale rule applies across all of them. Second, short-term lots bought within the last year should be left alone if possible, because a gain on them is taxed at ordinary rates.

Some lots are especially valuable to keep. Shares bought before 2011, and fund shares bought before 2012, are often noncovered: the broker is not required to report their basis to the IRS and may not know it. If you sell them, you have to prove the basis yourself. The older the lot, the more important it is to keep the purchase records.
FIFO is only the default. If you want to sell specific lots, choose them at the latest when the trade settles, either through a standing method at the broker or in the order itself.

## Moving an account to another broker

Moving securities to another broker in your own name has no tax consequences. Transfers usually run through ACATS, the automated transfer system, and the shares arrive with their original purchase dates. The transferring broker must pass on the basis information for covered securities in a transfer statement (26 U.S.C. § 6045A). Many brokers charge a fee for an outgoing transfer, and many receiving brokers offer to reimburse it.

The situation is different if the securities pass to another person. A gift is not a sale, so it does not trigger tax at the time of the transfer, but the basis and the latent tax go with the shares. Transfers between spouses are not taxed and also keep the original basis (§ 1041). At death, the rules change completely: the heirs receive the shares with a basis equal to their value on the date of death (§ 1014).

bloecke.titel: Tax consequences when securities leave an account
bloecke.unter: Only a sale triggers income tax. What matters for later is the basis the shares carry with them.

bloecke.md:
If the new broker does not have the basis, the Form 1099-B for a later sale will show it as not reported. This typically happens with very old positions, shares from employee stock plans, paper certificates and transfers from abroad. You must then enter the basis yourself, and if you cannot document it, the IRS can treat the basis as unproven.

For a position with $10,000 of proceeds and a real gain of $1,000, the difference between a documented basis and a basis of zero is $150 versus $1,500 of tax at 15%. Keep trade confirmations, year-end statements and records of reinvested dividends for as long as you hold the shares, and after that for as long as the return for the year of sale can be examined.

## Gifts and inheritances

In the case of a gift, the recipient takes over the donor's basis and holding period (§ 1015). A gift therefore does not reset the entry price; the latent tax passes to the recipient. If the shares are worth less than the donor's basis at the time of the gift, a special rule applies: for calculating a later loss, the recipient's basis is the lower market value. Gifts of up to $19,000 per recipient per year do not require a gift tax return; above that, Form 709 is due, but tax is only owed after the lifetime exemption of $15,000,000 per person in 2026 has been used up.

A gift can still save tax if the recipient has a lower rate, for example an adult child whose gains fall into the 0% range. For minors and many students, however, the kiddie tax applies. A gift of long-term appreciated shares to a public charity is even more effective: if you itemize, you can generally deduct their full market value, up to 30% of your adjusted gross income, and neither you nor the charity pays tax on the gain.

At death, the basis of inherited shares is stepped up, or down, to their market value on the date of death (§ 1014). The heirs can sell immediately with little or no gain, and their holding period is treated as long-term. In community property states, both halves of a married couple's community property receive the new basis when the first spouse dies. For older investors with large gains, holding until death can therefore be worth more than any sale or gift.

## Timing of the sale and tax deferral

As long as nothing is sold, the part of the portfolio that economically belongs to the government also remains invested and earns returns. This works like an interest-free loan whose value grows with the holding period.

An illustrative calculation with $100,000 of starting capital, a gross return of 7% a year and a term of 30 years shows the order of magnitude. Realized gains are taxed at 15%; dividends are ignored for simplicity. If you sell only at the end, $662,042 remains after tax. If the portfolio is turned over completely every year, it is $566,277, with the same gross return and the same tax rate. The difference of around $96,000 corresponds to 0.55 percentage points of net return a year. If the shares are held until death and the heirs receive a stepped-up basis, the full $761,226 remains free of income tax.

bloecke.md:
Two qualifications apply to this calculation.

First, dividends and fund distributions limit the effect. They are taxed every year, whether or not you sell. With a dividend yield of 1.5% and a 15% rate, around 0.2% of the portfolio goes to tax every year, and only the price gains remain deferred. Index ETFs keep this part small because they rarely distribute capital gains.

Second, deferral is not exemption, except through the step-up at death or a gift to charity. Advertising that promises to “save tax” usually means “pay tax later”. The advantage lies in the compound return on the deferred amount, not in the amount itself. It also assumes that the rate does not rise before the sale; tax rates and the step-up rule depend on future legislation and cannot be hedged.

The deferral advantage argues against unnecessary turnover. However, it is no reason to keep a wrong position. A portfolio that is not cleaned up purely for tax reasons continues to carry a concentration risk, and the tax argument does nothing to change that.

Conversely, switching to a fund that is only slightly cheaper often does not pay off. With a position worth $100,000 and an unrealized gain of $40,000, the switch immediately costs 40,000 × 15% = $6,000 in federal tax. An expense ratio that is 0.10 percentage points lower brings $100 a year. Direct new contributions to the cheaper fund instead, and switch inside a 401(k) or IRA, where it costs no tax.

- Set the cost basis method at your broker before you sell, for example specific identification with a standing “highest cost” or tax-optimized order.
- Before every partial sale, look at the lots and their holding periods, and avoid selling short-term lots with gains.
- Keep purchase records permanently, especially for shares bought before 2011, fund shares bought before 2012 and positions transferred between brokers.
- If you give to charity, consider giving long-term appreciated shares instead of cash.
- Heirs should document the market value on the date of death; it is the new basis.

mitnehmen: A long holding period does not make gains tax-free, but it defers the tax until the sale, and that is where the advantage lies; at death, the step-up in basis can remove the gain entirely.
FIFO is only the default: with specific identification, chosen by the time the trade settles, you can sell the lots with the highest basis first.
Moving securities to another broker in your own name does not trigger tax; the basis must be passed on, and for noncovered lots you have to prove it yourself.
A gift passes the basis and the latent tax to the recipient; an inheritance resets the basis to the value at death; a gift of appreciated shares to charity avoids the tax on the gain.
In the 30-year illustrative calculation, around 0.55 percentage points of net return a year depend solely on whether the portfolio is turned over.

begriffe.text: Method of choosing which lots are sold in a partial sale, chosen at the latest when the trade settles (26 CFR § 1.1012-1(c)). Without it, the shares bought first are treated as sold first.
Rule under which inherited property receives a basis equal to its market value on the date of death (26 U.S.C. § 1014). Gains accrued during the deceased's lifetime are never subject to income tax.

Rule under which the recipient of a gift takes over the donor's basis and holding period (26 U.S.C. § 1015). For a later loss, the basis is limited to the market value at the time of the gift if that was lower.

Security for which the broker must report the basis to the IRS on Form 1099-B: generally stock acquired from 2011 and fund shares acquired from 2012. For older, noncovered lots, the investor must document the basis.

Tax not yet due on unrealized gains. It appears on no statement but reduces the value at the investor's disposal after tax; at a 15% rate, about 85 cents of every dollar of long-term gain belong to the investor.
